title: Complex Numbers
body:
A **complex number** is $z = a + bi$, where $a$ is the **real part** $\text{Re}(z)$, $b$ is the
**imaginary part** $\text{Im}(z)$, and $i$ is the imaginary unit defined by

$$
i^2 = -1
$$

That single definition is the whole extension. $\mathbb{R}$ is closed under addition,
subtraction, multiplication, and division but not under taking roots: $x^2 = -1$ has no real
solution. Adjoin one and you get $\mathbb{C}$, in which **every polynomial of degree $n$ has
exactly $n$ roots**. That is the fundamental theorem of algebra, and it is the reason complex
numbers are on a linear algebra syllabus rather than being a curiosity.

## Why a linear algebra course covers them

Because the characteristic polynomial of a real matrix can fail to have real roots. Rotation by
$90°$ is

$$
\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix},
\qquad \det(A - \lambda I) = \lambda^2 + 1
$$

with roots $\pm i$. Geometrically obvious in hindsight: a rotation leaves **no** real direction
unchanged, so there is no real eigenvector to find. Working in $\mathbb{C}$ means every square
matrix has a full set of [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]], and **complex eigenvalues are how a
matrix says "I rotate"**. Their imaginary part is the rotation rate, which is why an oscillating
solution to a system of [[Differential Equations]] comes from a complex eigenvalue.

## Arithmetic

Treat $i$ as a symbol you can do algebra with, and replace $i^2$ by $-1$ whenever it appears.

$$
(a+bi) + (c+di) = (a+c) + (b+d)i
$$

$$
(a+bi)(c+di) = ac + adi + bci + bdi^2 = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i
$$

Addition is componentwise, so **$\mathbb{C}$ is $\mathbb{R}^2$ as far as addition is
concerned**, and $a + bi$ plots as the point $(a,b)$ in the **complex plane**. What makes it
more than $\mathbb{R}^2$ is that it has a multiplication, and multiplication is a rotation and a
scaling. That reading is [[Polar Form]]'s job.

Powers of $i$ cycle with period four: $i, -1, -i, 1$, then repeat. So $i^{403} = i^{400}i^3 =
-i$.

## Conjugate

The **conjugate** of $z = a+bi$ is $\bar{z} = a - bi$: same real part, flipped imaginary part, a
reflection across the real axis. Its use is that

$$
z\bar{z} = (a+bi)(a-bi) = a^2 + b^2
$$

which is **real and non-negative**. That number is $|z|^2$, the squared **modulus**, and
$|z| = \sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ is the distance from the origin: the same formula as the norm of a
[[Vector]] in $\mathbb{R}^2$, because it is the same distance.

**Division is the conjugate's main job.** To divide, multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of
the bottom, which makes the denominator real:

$$
\frac{3+2i}{1-i} = \frac{(3+2i)(1+i)}{(1-i)(1+i)} = \frac{3 + 3i + 2i - 2}{2} = \frac{1+5i}{2}
$$

Same trick as rationalising a surd denominator.

Rules: $\overline{z+w} = \bar{z}+\bar{w}$, $\overline{zw} = \bar{z}\bar{w}$, and
$z = \bar{z}$ exactly when $z$ is real.

**Complex roots of real polynomials come in conjugate pairs.** If $z$ is a root, so is $\bar{z}$.
Which is why a real matrix's complex eigenvalues always arrive in pairs, and why a real cubic
always has at least one real root.

## As an algebraic structure

$\mathbb{C}$ is a **[[Field]]**: addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division by anything
non-zero all work. It is $\mathbb{R}$ extended by a root of $x^2+1$, which is the
[[Field Extension]] view [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]] takes ($\mathbb{C} = \mathbb{R}[x]/(x^2+1)$, so $i$
is a coset and $i^2 = -1$ is what reducing by $x^2+1$ does), and it sits in the vault's complex-numbers ladder: arithmetic
and geometry here, structure in Abstract Algebra, analysis in [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]].

There is a matrix realisation, which is a satisfying way to see that nothing mystical is
happening: $a + bi$ behaves identically to

$$
\begin{bmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a \end{bmatrix}
$$

under [[Matrix]] addition and [[Matrix Multiplication]]. $i$ corresponds to the $90°$ rotation
above, and $i^2 = -1$ is the statement that rotating twice by $90°$ negates.
